title: Amazing grace
hookLine: the fifth visit: a song everyone knows, written by a man who didn't think he deserved to sing it

lines: A SONG THAT LEFT THE CHURCH.
WHAT A CHRISTIAN MEANS BY GRACE.
cards: A church, any church: stone or strip mall, a choir or a guitar. Sooner or later someone starts a song that long ago walked out of church and into the wider world. Amazing grace, how sweet the sound.
It was published in England in 1779, by John Newton, a clergyman who had once worked in the Atlantic slave trade, and who later, publicly, turned against it.
When he wrote about a grace that saved a wretch, he wasn't being modest. He meant it. Today, what a Christian means by grace.

teach.b: The New Testament's word is Greek: charis. It means a gift, a favor, something given freely. So first, grace is a gift you didn't earn.
Paul puts it plainly in his letter to the Ephesians. In the King James Version: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God."
Not a wage. A gift. Second, grace finds people at their weakest, not their best.

Paul writes that he begged the Lord three times to take away something he calls a thorn in the flesh, and heard this answer: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness."
That's why Newton could sing it. Grace, for Christians, isn't a prize for the ones who got it right. It's what meets the ones who didn't.

teach.h: CHURCHES DIFFER ON HOW IT WORKS.
teach.b: Third, Christians differ on how grace works, and they say so.
Catholic and Orthodox Christians teach that grace comes especially through the sacraments, like baptism and communion, and that a person freely cooperates with it.
Many Protestants stress grace alone: God's gift, received by faith, with good works flowing from it rather than earning it. Now, from your own door. Hindus have words for this too.
Kripa is grace, and the sweet you're handed at the temple is prasad, which also means grace, a favor freely given.

Krishna himself speaks of devotees reaching him by his grace. The honest difference: for Christians, grace comes through Jesus Christ, his life, his death and his rising. That's the center of their house.

how: Christians speak of grace in sermons, hymns and prayers, and many say grace before meals; Catholic and Orthodox Christians receive grace especially through the sacraments, while many Protestants emphasize grace received through faith.

o: God's gift of love and help, freely given
a reward God gives to people who behave well
elegance and ease in the way someone moves

p: by grace are ye saved through faith

s: for Christians, grace is a reward for being good
Paul calls it the gift of God: not a wage, not of yourselves.
all Christians describe how grace works in the same way
Catholic and Orthodox Christians stress the sacraments and cooperation; many Protestants stress grace alone, through faith.
the temple sweet called prasad also means grace
prasad is a favor freely given. for Christians, grace comes through Jesus Christ; that's the honest difference.

games.q: you're Paul. you've begged God three times to take away a thorn in the flesh. what answer does the letter say you heard?
o: it will be gone by morning.
my grace is sufficient for thee.
games.why: the thorn stays. the answer is grace: my strength is made perfect in weakness. grace meets people at their weakest.

practice: Bring to mind one good thing in your life you didn't earn, not your job, not your effort, but something given: a friend who stayed, a morning you woke up well, a person who forgave you before you asked.
Let yourself receive it without explaining why you deserve it, and notice what that's like. If you pray, you can say thank you in your own way.

wordCard.voice: Charis, a gift, a favor, freely given, love that isn't earned.

orig.note: Greek charis, grace: a gift or favor freely given; it sits in a family of words for joy and thanks.

carryVoice: Your line: grace, love you didn't earn. Five houses now, each heard in its own words.
